How LaunchPad works

The LaunchPad stack.

Get your first post out with a crew. Keep showing up for each other through the releases that follow.

  1. 01 · Crew

    Build your crew

    Start with founders who get what you’re building.

    Look for people who know your space or work with the same audience. They can spot use cases you missed and know who might find your post helpful.

    See an example crew ↗

  2. 02 · Brief

    Share a clear brief

    One short demo and one specific ask.

    Explain who the post is for, show what’s new, and tell the crew how they can help. Give them enough context to write in their own voice.

    Use the sample brief ↗

  3. 03 · Timing

    Schedule the first hour

    One shared window across time zones.

    Pick an hour your crew can make and include the time zone. If you publish at 14:00 UTC, everyone knows to look out for the link then and when you’ll be there to answer.

    See the first-hour playbook ↗

  4. 04 · Live

    Get the conversation going

    Give readers a way into the post.

    Send the link when you publish. Crew members can leave a useful question, like what resonates, or share the post with someone who would use what you built.

    Explore example posts ↗

  5. 05 · Next launch

    Return the favor

    Keep showing up after launch day.

    Take a turn supporting someone else’s release. Keep the crew in the loop as you ship features, share progress, or ask for feedback on what comes next.

    See what comes next ↗

The launch playbook

Make the first hour count.

One shared window gives your crew time to understand what you’re launching and a clear way to help.

  1. 01 / Before you post

    Pick a window together.

    Choose an hour that works for your crew across time zones. Tell them what you’re shipping and who it’s for.

  2. 02 / When you go live

    Put the post in front of your crew.

    Share the link when it’s live. Founders can reply in their own words, like what resonates, or share it with people who’d care.

  3. 03 / On their launch day

    Return the favor.

    Make time for another founder’s post when it’s their turn. Bring the same attention you’d want for your own launch.

Before you publish

Give your crew the context.

A short brief saves everyone from guessing. Tell them who the post is for, show the part worth paying attention to, and make one clear ask.

  • Say who it’s for. Name the person who has this problem.
  • Show what changed. Send the clip, screenshot, or quick example that makes it click.
  • Be specific about help. Ask for a share, a question, or feedback where it’s relevant.
  • Confirm the window. Share the time and time zone, then drop the link when it’s live.

Example launch brief

A client portal for freelancers

Who it’s for
Freelancers chasing feedback across email and chat.
What to look at
A 20-second demo of one draft going from review to approved.
How to help
If you know someone who works this way, send it to them with your own take.
When it goes live
Thursday at 14:00 UTC.

FAQ

Before you post.

What’s a LaunchPad crew?

A small group of founders who agree to show up during one another’s launch windows. Each founder shares their post and gives the group enough context to start a real conversation.

Why focus on the first hour?

A shared window gives your crew a clear time to read and respond while the announcement is fresh. How far the post travels depends on the post, the audience, and the platform.

Can we coordinate across time zones?

Yes. Agree on a window that works for your crew, and include the time zone when you share your launch time.

Is this just for product launches?

You can use the same approach for feature releases, progress updates, and other milestones when you’d like founders to help start the conversation.

What should I send before the post is live?

Send four things your crew can skim quickly: who it’s for, what’s new, when it goes live, and one way to help. A short demo can make the post easier to share.

Do we all have to share every post?

Pick the response that adds something. A useful question, firsthand perspective, or introduction to the right person can be more relevant than a share.

What happens after the first hour?

Keep answering questions on your post, take note of what people asked about, and check when someone else in your crew is shipping next.
